data.about:
Josh Janow is at the forefront of harnessing the power of social media and open-source data as the Chief Executive Officer of SMI Aware. His company specializes in the research, collection, and preservation of social media and other publicly available information, aiding legal, HR, and risk and compliance teams in discovery, due diligence, and risk management initiatives. Josh's leadership at SMI Aware embodies his conviction that timely and accurate data access significantly enhances decision-making processes, risk management, and overall business outcomes.

Throughout his expansive career, Josh has consistently championed the transformative impact of data on strategic decision-making, whether on the operational floor or in the legal department. At SMI Aware, he leads his team in uncovering vital data, often acting as the "corner piece" to the complex puzzles faced by clients. This commitment empowers clients with critical insights that shape their strategic landscapes.

Before ascending to his current role, Josh's journey included significant legal and executive tenures, notably as General Counsel and later as President of the North American division of gategroup. There, he led a $1 billion revenue operation with over 10,000 employees, navigating the division through the industry's most volatile periods. His strategic initiatives there—ranging from drastic restructuring during the COVID-19 pandemic to securing substantial new business and fostering a data-centric corporate culture—have left a lasting impact on the industry.

Josh started his career at Weil, Gotshal & Manges, where he honed his skills in legal and strategic business management, setting the stage for his later achievements in executive leadership.

data.about:
Some things I believe (but I'm open to learning that I am wrong):  
*AI doesn't exist; Machine Intelligence does. 
*Measure, don't speculate. 
*Real people have emotions and want to align their reasoning with their feelings. 
*Occasionally challenge everything you think you know, especially what you are sure about. 
*Smart failure is limited and leads to learning; Dumb failure is just failure. 
*Your #1 job is to decide what deserves your attention and what doesn't, and to allocate your time and money accordingly. 
*If you succeed all the time, you probably aren't trying enough new things. 
*Almost all data analytics problems follow a predictable course.
*Facts and beliefs are different categories; Learn to distinguish.
*Everyone has something to offer someone else.
*Being the best isn't really necessary or important; Being your best is.
*Numeracy is key to most business decisions

data.about:
‎‎‎‎‎‎‎‎‎I love listening to TEDx Talks and tech talks like Machine Learning Street Talks. I have a deep passion for mathematics; my favourite scientist is Isaac Newton. I admire Steve Jobs's multifaceted personality. In my free time, I enjoy watching Sheldon Cooper and other English TV shows to improve my English.

I consider myself a strict person; I never smile at someone I don’t like, and my facial expressions always reflect my true feelings.

Currently, I am working on ocean modeling, where we have created a digital twin of the ocean. The problem I am solving is fascinating: recovering the stream function of the ocean from partial sequential (real-time) observations, known as drifters or Lagrangian tracers in ocean science. Essentially, it's about predicting ocean waves on large scales, such as 100 km x 100 km, over extended periods like six months.

This work is crucial for climate science and weather forecasting. Understanding ocean behavior, which is stochastic and turbulent, is akin to predicting chaos. This endeavor is incredibly exciting as it may one day contribute to solving the Navier-Stokes equation, one of the seven Millennium Problems in mathematics. Who knows what possibilities might unfold from there? It could lead to a new revolution in the Applied theory of everything, enabling us to model any dynamical system in any field.

My work feels like learning a new language—the language of the universe, the language of God. I always work with two pictures: the truth, derived from physics or real oceanic data (which I hope to incorporate in the future), and the recovery, produced by our algorithms or filters. It's like comparing a photograph taken with a brand-new iPhone to a hand-drawn image by an artist—the recovery is the artist’s rendition, and the artist is the algorithm or me :)

Thesis Title
Advanced Data-Driven Filtering Techniques for Turbulent Flow Modelling: A Lagrangian Data Assimilation Framework

Research Scope
Rigorous development of hybrid filtering methodologies to perform uncertainty quantification and state estimation in high-dimensional, nonlinear dynamical systems. The framework renders Lagrangian particle-based observational strategies to reconstruct turbulent geophysical flows, with a primary application to the barotropic Quasi-Geostrophic (QG) equation under sparse and noisy conditions.

Programming & Numerical Modeling: Python (NumPy, SciPy, PyTorch), MATLAB (for prototyping PDE solvers and spectral models)

Data Assimilation Algorithms: Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF), Particle Filter (PF), hybrid EnKF–PF methods

HPC Workflows: Parallel computing on cluster-based environments; optimized matrix operations and ensemble simulations

data.about: I graduated from Hanahan High School as the valedictorian in 2019 and graduated cum laude from Clemson University Honors College with a B.S. in Bioengineering with a concentration in biomaterials in May of 2023.  I then graduated from Clemson University with a M.S. in Bioengineering with a thesis on developing a cost-affordable thin-layer chromatography testing kit for falsified and substandard pharmaceuticals in Tanzania.  During my undergraduate degree, I was on an electrospinning research team for 3 years.  Through this research, I had the opportunity to present at state and global conferences, work on a literature review, and gain a great deal of laboratory skills.  For my senior year capstone project, my team designed a size-convertible medical backboard that can accommodate a greater percentage of the population than a current backboard to allow safety for patients of all sizes.  With our pitch and design, we won first place at the Clemson Spark Challenge Competition as well as the Spiro Institute's Pitch Smackdown Competition.  During my graduate degree, I mentored several undergraduate researchers, attended and presented at conferences, and had the opportunity to visit Tanzania and discuss my research with our partner university, Arusha Technical College.

My passion lies at the intersection between research and policy where there is the most hope to achieve a healthy and sustainable future for our posterity.

As a recent graduate from the Biosystems Engineering major at Clemson University, with an emphasis on Ecological Engineering, I studied various methods to clean both soil and water in a way that is both economical and effective for developing countries to implement. Despite graduating, I still stay up-to-date on bioremediation research and development. 

In addition to my interest in research, I hope to extend my knowledge to the government sector. There is an overwhelming amount of research proving the efficacy of sustainable initiatives, yet excess waste and environmental racism continue to plague our developed society. I believe there can be no progress unless such research can be advocated for in a setting where both the voters and public officials can understand the benefits of such green practices and demand their implementation.

From this internship, I learned about stem cell research regarding cardiac development, how to use florescence to record data of cells contracting, and how to use a combination of MATLAB and Leica Application Suite X to analyze this data.

data.about:
Dr. Thomas Britt is a Professor of Psychology at Clemson University, a Faculty Instructor at the US Army War College, and the Editor-in-Chief of Military Psychology. He received his Ph.D. from the University of Florida in 1994 in Social Psychology before entering active duty as a research psychologist in the U.S. Army.  He was stationed at the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research (WRAIR) from 1994 to 1999, and then spent a year at King College before moving to Clemson University in 2000, where he was promoted to Full Professor in 2007.  He has published over 100 empirical articles, is the author on two books related to Organizational Psychology and Employee Stress, and has been an editor for two books and a 4-volume series in the area of Military Psychology.  His articles have been published in leading journals such as the Harvard Business Review, Psychological Review, Psychological Bulletin, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, Journal of Organizational Behavior, Journal of Personality, and the Journal of Occupational Health Psychology.   His current research programs investigate how stigma and other barriers to care influence employees in high-stress occupations seeking needed mental health treatment, and the identification of factors that promote resilience among employees in high-stress occupations. His research has been funded by multiple grants and contracts from the Department of Defense and the Intelligence Community.   

For a complete description of current research programs, please visit his website at: https://www.clemson.edu/cbshs/about/profiles/index.html?userid=TWBRITT and https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&user=hlEVHFEAAAAJ

data.about: My research interests focus primarily on aversive interpersonal behaviors, most notably complaining, teasing and bullying. Over the past few years, I have also investigated school and mass shootings. In the past couple of years, I have examined the role of psychological mattering, or its converse antimattering, as it relates to aversive interpersonal behaviors. I am the author or co-author of over 20 books including Complaining, Teasing, and Other Annoying Behaviors; Aversive Interpersonal Behaviors; Behaving Badly, The Social Psychology of Emotional and Behavioral Problems; and Cyberbullying: Bullying in the Digital Age. In addition to research, I love teaching students at Clemson University. I have received several awards including the Provost Senior Award for Excellence in Teaching, the Phil Prince Award for Excellence and Innovation in the Classroom, Clemson University’s College of Business and Behavioral Science Senior Research Award, Clemson University's College of Social, Behavioral, and Health Sciences Senior Scholar Award, and Clemson Women’s Commission Outstanding Female Faculty Member.
